concepts.name: Definition and types of matrices
concepts.oneLineSummary: Rectangular array; row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero, symmetric, skew-symmetric.

concepts.name: Equality of matrices
concepts.oneLineSummary: Two matrices equal if same order and corresponding elements equal.

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction of matrices
concepts.oneLineSummary: Defined only for same order; element-wise; commutative and associative.

concepts.name: Scalar multiplication
concepts.oneLineSummary: Each element multiplied by the scalar; distributive over addition.

concepts.name: Matrix multiplication
concepts.oneLineSummary: Defined when columns of first equal rows of second; not commutative in general.

concepts.name: Transpose of a matrix
concepts.oneLineSummary: Rows become columns; (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A; (A+B)ᵀ = Aᵀ+Bᵀ; (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

concepts.name: Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
concepts.oneLineSummary: Aᵀ = A (symmetric); Aᵀ = −A (skew-symmetric); every square matrix = symmetric + skew-symmetric.

concepts.name: Determinant of a square matrix
concepts.oneLineSummary: Scalar associated with square matrix; det(AB)=det(A)det(B); det(Aᵀ)=det(A).

concepts.name: Adjoint and inverse of a matrix
concepts.oneLineSummary: adj(A) = transpose of cofactor matrix; A⁻¹ = (1/det A) adj(A) when det A ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Singular and non-singular matrices
concepts.oneLineSummary: Singular if det = 0 (no inverse); non-singular if det ≠ 0 (invertible).

concepts.name: System of linear equations in matrix form
concepts.oneLineSummary: AX = B; unique solution X = A⁻¹B when A non-singular.

concepts.name: Cramer's rule
concepts.oneLineSummary: Solution of n equations via ratios of determinants.

concepts.name: Elementary row and column operations
concepts.oneLineSummary: Used to find rank, inverse, or reduce to echelon form.

concepts.name: Rank of a matrix
concepts.oneLineSummary: Maximum number of linearly independent rows (or columns); equals order of largest non-zero minor.

concepts.name: Properties of determinants
concepts.oneLineSummary: Interchange of rows changes sign; repeated row → zero; linear combination of rows leaves det unchanged.

qna.question: Define a matrix and list five important types of square matrices.
qna.answer: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Important square types are: diagonal matrix (non-zero entries only on the main diagonal), scalar matrix (diagonal with equal entries), identity matrix (diagonal of 1’s), symmetric matrix (Aᵀ = A) and skew-symmetric matrix (Aᵀ = −A).

qna.question: When are two matrices said to be equal?
qna.answer: Two matrices are equal if and only if they have the same order (same number of rows and columns) and their corresponding elements are equal. Equality is an element-wise notion.

qna.question: State the conditions under which two matrices can be added and the properties of matrix addition.
qna.answer: Addition is defined only when the matrices have the same order. The sum is obtained by adding corresponding elements. Matrix addition is commutative (A+B=B+A) and associative ((A+B)+C=A+(B+C)). The zero matrix is the additive identity.

qna.question: When is the product AB defined and is matrix multiplication commutative?
qna.answer: The product AB is defined when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. In general AB ≠ BA even when both products exist. Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive over addition, but not commutative.

qna.question: State three important properties of the transpose of a matrix.
qna.answer: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A; (A+B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ; (AB)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ. The last property shows that transposition reverses the order of a product. Also det(Aᵀ) = det(A).

qna.question: Define symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices and state the decomposition of a square matrix.
qna.answer: A is symmetric if Aᵀ = A and skew-symmetric if Aᵀ = −A. Every square matrix A can be uniquely written as the sum of a symmetric matrix (A+Aᵀ)/2 and a skew-symmetric matrix (A−Aᵀ)/2.

qna.question: State two fundamental properties of determinants.
qna.answer: det(AB) = det(A) det(B) and det(Aᵀ) = det(A). Consequently a matrix and its transpose have the same determinant, and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants.

qna.question: How is the inverse of a square matrix obtained using the adjoint?
qna.answer: If A is non-singular (det A ≠ 0) then A⁻¹ = (1/det A) · adj(A), where adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix of A. The identity A · adj(A) = (det A) I holds even when A is singular.

qna.question: What is the difference between a singular and a non-singular matrix?
qna.answer: A square matrix is singular if its determinant is zero; it has no inverse. A matrix is non-singular if its determinant is non-zero; it possesses a unique inverse. Invertibility is equivalent to non-singularity.

qna.question: Write a system of linear equations in matrix form and state the condition for a unique solution.
qna.answer: The system aᵢⱼ xⱼ = bᵢ is written AX = B where A is the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and B the column of constants. A unique solution exists if and only if A is non-singular; the solution is then X = A⁻¹ B.

qna.question: Give an example of a 2×2 identity matrix and a 2×2 zero matrix.
qna.answer: Identity: [[1,0],[0,1]]. Zero: [[0,0],[0,0]]. The identity acts as the multiplicative identity for square matrices of the same order; the zero matrix is the additive identity.

qna.question: Compute the product [[1,2],[3,4]] [[5,6],[7,8]].
qna.answer: First row first column: 1·5+2·7=19; first row second: 1·6+2·8=22; second row first: 3·5+4·7=43; second row second: 3·6+4·8=50. Product is [[19,22],[43,50]].

qna.question: If A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], write Aᵀ.
qna.answer: Aᵀ = [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]. The three columns of A become the three rows of Aᵀ. The order changes from 2×3 to 3×2.

qna.question: Show that the matrix [[0,2],[-2,0]] is skew-symmetric.
qna.answer: Its transpose is [[0,−2],[2,0]] which equals −A. Therefore Aᵀ = −A and the matrix is skew-symmetric. The diagonal elements of a real skew-symmetric matrix must be zero.

qna.question: Evaluate the determinant of [[2,3],[1,4]].
qna.answer: det = 2·4 − 3·1 = 8 − 3 = 5. For a 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] the determinant is ad − bc.

qna.question: Find the inverse of [[2,1],[5,3]] if it exists.
qna.answer: det = 6 − 5 = 1 ≠ 0, so inverse exists. Cofactors: C11=3, C12=−5, C21=−1, C22=2. adj(A)=[[3,−1],[−5,2]]. Inverse = adj(A) = [[3,−1],[−5,2]]. Verification: A times this matrix yields the identity.

qna.question: Is the matrix [[1,2],[2,4]] singular? Justify.
qna.answer: Yes. Its determinant is 1·4 − 2·2 = 0. A zero determinant means the matrix is singular and does not possess an inverse. The rows are linearly dependent (second row = 2 × first row).

qna.question: Solve the system 2x + y = 5, 3x + 2y = 8 by matrix inversion.
What is the rank of a matrix and how is it related to the existence of an inverse?
qna.answer: The rank is the maximum number of linearly independent rows (or columns). A square matrix of order n is invertible if and only if its rank equals n (full rank). Rank less than n implies the matrix is singular.

qna.question: State the effect on a determinant of interchanging two rows.
qna.answer: Interchanging two rows (or two columns) multiplies the determinant by −1. Consequently a matrix with two identical rows has determinant zero, because swapping those rows would leave the matrix unchanged yet change the sign of the determinant.

qna.question: If A = [[1,−2],[3,0]], compute 3A.
qna.answer: 3A = [[3,−6],[9,0]]. Every element of A is multiplied by the scalar 3. Scalar multiplication is distributive over matrix addition.

qna.question: Give an example of two matrices A and B such that AB ≠ BA.
qna.answer: Let A = [[1,1],[0,0]], B = [[0,0],[1,1]]. Then AB = [[1,1],[0,0]] while BA = [[0,0],[1,1]]. The products are different, illustrating non-commutativity.

qna.question: Prove that the diagonal elements of a real skew-symmetric matrix are zero.
qna.answer: Let A be skew-symmetric, so Aᵀ = −A. Looking at the diagonal entries, aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ, which forces 2aᵢᵢ = 0 and therefore aᵢᵢ = 0. All diagonal entries vanish.

qna.question: Show that A · adj(A) = (det A) I for a 2×2 matrix.
qna.answer: For A = [[a,b],[c,d]], adj(A) = [[d,−b],[−c,a]]. The product is [[ad−bc,0],[0,ad−bc]] = (det A) I. The same identity holds for matrices of any order.

qna.question: State Cramer’s rule for a system of two equations in two unknowns.
qna.answer: For a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂, if Δ = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0, then x = Δₓ/Δ, y = Δᵧ/Δ where Δₓ is the determinant obtained by replacing the first column by the constants and Δᵧ by replacing the second column.

qna.question: What are elementary row operations and why are they useful?
qna.answer: The three elementary row operations are: swapping two rows, multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar, and adding a multiple of one row to another. They are used to reduce a matrix to row-echelon form, to compute its rank, and to find its inverse by the Gauss-Jordan method.

qna.question: Find the rank of the matrix [[1,2,3],[2,4,6],[3,6,9]].
qna.answer: All rows are multiples of the first row, so the row space is one-dimensional. The rank is 1. Equivalently every 2×2 minor vanishes while at least one 1×1 minor is non-zero.

qna.question: If two rows of a matrix are identical, what is its determinant?
qna.answer: The determinant is zero. Swapping the two identical rows leaves the matrix unchanged, yet the interchange multiplies the determinant by −1; the only number equal to its own negative is zero.

qna.question: Evaluate det([[1,2,3],[0,4,5],[0,0,6]]).
qna.answer: The matrix is upper triangular, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: 1·4·6 = 24. For any triangular matrix the determinant equals the product of the diagonal elements.

qna.question: If A is m×n and B is n×p, what is the order of AB?
qna.answer: The product AB is an m×p matrix. The inner dimensions n cancel, leaving the outer dimensions m and p as the order of the product.

qna.question: Prove that (AB)ᵀ = Bᵀ Aᵀ.
qna.answer: The (i,j)-entry of (AB)ᵀ is the (j,i)-entry of AB, which is the sum over k of a_{jk} b_{ki}. The same sum is the (i,j)-entry of Bᵀ Aᵀ. Therefore the two matrices are equal. The order of multiplication is reversed by transposition.

qna.question: A student computes A⁻¹ = adj(A) without dividing by det A. When is this correct?
qna.answer: It is correct only when det A = ±1. In general the factor 1/det A must be included. Omitting the factor is a common error that produces a matrix whose product with A is (det A)I rather than I.

qna.question: If AX = B has a unique solution, what can be said about the homogeneous system AX = 0?
qna.answer: The homogeneous system has only the trivial solution X = 0. Uniqueness for the non-homogeneous system is equivalent to the coefficient matrix being invertible, which forces the homogeneous system to have only the zero solution.

qna.question: What is a scalar matrix? Give an example of order 3.
qna.answer: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix in which all diagonal entries are equal. An example of order 3 is [[5,0,0],[0,5,0],[0,0,5]] = 5 I₃. Every scalar matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity.

qna.question: If the rank of a 3×3 matrix is 2, can it be invertible?
qna.answer: No. Invertibility requires full rank, i.e., rank equal to the order of the matrix. Rank 2 < 3 implies the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

qna.question: How does adding a multiple of one row to another row affect the determinant?
qna.answer: The determinant remains unchanged. This property is the basis of many evaluation techniques: one can clear entries without altering the value of the determinant, simplifying subsequent expansion.

qna.question: If A and B are matrices of the same order and k is a scalar, prove that k(A+B) = kA + kB.
qna.answer: The (i,j)-entry of the left side is k(a_{ij}+b_{ij}) = k a_{ij} + k b_{ij}, which is precisely the (i,j)-entry of the right side. The equality holds element-wise and therefore as matrices.
